title: Vortex identification asks whether the local flow rotates or strains, and where the threshold is drawn
summary: Vorticity alone cannot tell a vortex from a shear layer. The Okubo-Weiss parameter and the Q-criterion compare rotation with strain point by point; the Q-R diagram and the quadrant plot compress the same kind of information into statistics, at the price of losing position.

media.alt: Two square maps of a 2D turbulence snapshot. Left: vorticity with a red-blue colour bar from minus 8 to 8, showing blobs of both signs and thin filaments. Right: Okubo-Weiss segmentation in three classes: dark blue vortex-dominated patches clustered around the strongest vorticity blobs, a few dark red strain-dominated cells, and a large white ambiguous background.

source.caption: Vorticity field and Okubo-Weiss coherent-structure segmentation
source.note: Group explainer. The other three figures are the Q-criterion with line integral convolution, the joint Q-R distribution, and the quadrant decomposition of the shear-stress correlation. All are computed from one decaying 2D turbulence snapshot, so classic 3D or wall-bounded interpretations (teardrop, ejections and sweeps) do not apply literally; the project text discloses this for the quadrant figure.

read_the_figure.question: Which parts of the flow are dominated by rotation (coherent vortices) and which by strain, and is that more informative than the vorticity map?
read_the_figure.axes: Both panels share the x and y position axes of one periodic square. Left colour: vorticity in 1/s. Right colour: a three-class label (vortex, ambiguous, strain) from the sign and size of the Okubo-Weiss parameter.
look_at: Match the dark blue patches of the right panel to the strongest blobs of the left panel (for example near x = 2.4, y = 5.8). Strong rotation is classified as vortex.
Find places where the left panel shows an elongated filament of vorticity but the right panel is white or red. A strong shear layer has vorticity but no closed rotation.
The red cells are strain-dominated: look at where they sit relative to the blue patches (often between two vortices).
Estimate the share of white. If the background is mostly ambiguous, the result depends strongly on the chosen threshold.
In the Q-criterion panel the white area is Q below zero, and in the LIC panel texture lines follow the velocity direction; closed loops of texture mark vortices.
read_the_figure.proves: A point is rotation-dominated when the rotation rate exceeds the strain rate there. The map shows where that holds and groups those points into coherent regions. It does not by itself show that those regions persist in time or carry the energy.
if_wrong: A very noisy right panel with isolated single cells: the field is too coarse or the gradients are computed on grid-scale noise. Smooth first, or use a threshold tied to the standard deviation.
A segmentation that depends on an unstated threshold: a different cut-off makes a different set of vortices. Always state it.
Using a 3D picture on a 2D field: the Q-R teardrop and the ejection and sweep names come from 3D or wall-bounded flows. In 2D the third invariant R vanishes identically.
Quadrant fractions above 100 percent or below zero: the net shear stress is small and the ratio is unstable, not a sign of an error in the quadrants themselves.
must_check: The definition: W = S_n^2 + S_s^2 - omega^2 (negative inside vortices), or Q = minus W over four, and which sign the colour bar calls vortex.
The threshold used for the three classes, and the grid resolution.
That the field is truly 2D incompressible before using the identities in the steps.
For the Q-R plot, how R was computed and the colour bar's meaning (counts, not probability).
For the quadrant plot, whether the flow has a mean shear; if not, names such as ejection are only labels.
as_drawn: Vorticity colour bar about minus 8 to plus 8. The Q-criterion panel's maximum is about 38 per second squared.

Quadrant fractions of the net shear stress: outward interaction about minus 0.86, ejection about plus 1.48, inward interaction about minus 1.18, sweep about plus 1.56. They sum to 1.00 by construction (computed).
The Q-R histogram is concentrated at the origin with a maximum count near 1100 per cell; R spans about minus 27 to 18 and Q about minus 18 to 7 on the axes, almost all of it empty.

terms.meaning: The matrix of all first derivatives of velocity. It splits into a symmetric part (strain) and an antisymmetric part (rotation).
S_ij is the symmetric part of A, Omega_ij the antisymmetric part. In 2D the rotation rate is half the vorticity.
Squared strain minus squared vorticity, in 2D. Negative where rotation dominates.
Half the difference between the squared rotation and strain magnitudes. A vortex is where Q is positive.
A texture made by smearing noise along streamlines so that the direction of the flow is visible everywhere without choosing seed points.
The second and third invariants of the velocity-gradient tensor. Their joint distribution classifies local flow topology.
Splitting the product of two velocity fluctuations by the signs of the two fluctuations into four classes, each with its share of the correlation.
A region of the flow that keeps its identity for longer than the local eddy turnover time.

remember: Vorticity is not the same as a vortex: a shear layer has vorticity but no closed swirl.
For a 2D incompressible field, Q = minus W over four (checked by computing it for random gradients).
Eigenvalues of the 2D velocity-gradient matrix are plus and minus the square root of minus Q: imaginary (rotation) when Q is positive, real (strain) when Q is negative.
A segmentation is a threshold choice; state the threshold.
A Q-R plot discards position; a map discards statistics.
Quadrant fractions add to one, but a small denominator can push single fractions beyond 100 percent.

understand.title: Why vorticity maps mislead
understand.text: Vorticity is the sum of local rotation, whether the flow swirls or merely shears. A boundary layer has high vorticity and no vortex. Okubo and Weiss compared the strain and rotation contributions, and the Q-criterion does the same with the full velocity-gradient tensor. In 2D incompressible flow they are the same quantity up to a constant factor, so the second map adds no new information, only a different name.

understand.title: Maps against statistics
understand.text: The segmentation shows where, the Q-R histogram and the quadrant bars show how much and of which kind. The group therefore pairs spatial figures with two statistical summaries of the same field, and each hides what the other shows.

understand.title: A caution on borrowed pictures
understand.text: The Q-R teardrop and the ejection-sweep scheme are results for 3D and wall-bounded turbulence. Here they are applied to a 2D snapshot as a diagnostic exercise. Reading them in that spirit avoids drawing conclusions about wall turbulence from them.

steps.title: Strain and rotation in 2D
steps.tex: S_n=\partial_x u-\partial_y v,\qquad S_s=\partial_x v+\partial_y u,\qquad \omega=\partial_x v-\partial_y u
steps.note: Normal strain, shear strain and vorticity. These three numbers are all the information in the 2D velocity-gradient matrix of an incompressible flow beyond the divergence, which is zero.

steps.title: The Okubo-Weiss parameter
steps.note: Substituting v_y = minus u_x. W is negative when rotation beats strain. Segmentations typically choose a threshold at a fraction of the standard deviation of W; the stated value is part of the result.

steps.title: Q from the gradient tensor
steps.note: With the standard definitions above the factor is one quarter. The project caption quotes a factor of one half, which would hold under a different normalisation of the Okubo-Weiss parameter; check which one is used before comparing numbers across papers.

steps.title: Eigenvalues tell the topology
steps.note: Cayley-Hamilton for a traceless 2 by 2 matrix. For Q positive the eigenvalues are imaginary: nearby fluid circles around the point. For Q negative they are real: it is stretched along one direction and compressed along the other.

steps.title: Q and R in 3D, and why R vanishes in 2D
steps.note: In three dimensions the sign of the discriminant Delta separates focal from real eigenvalue topologies, and the joint PDF of Q and R takes the teardrop shape. If the velocity has no third component and no z-dependence, the third row and column of A are zero, so det A = 0 and R is identically zero: all points lie on the Q axis. A broad R spread in a 2D case therefore needs an explanation of how R was computed.

steps.title: The quadrant decomposition
steps.tex: \langle u'v'\rangle=\sum_{i=1}^{4}\langle u'v'\rangle_{i},\qquad f_i=\frac{\langle u'v'\rangle_i}{\langle u'v'\rangle},\qquad \sum_i f_i=1
steps.note: Quadrants are the four sign combinations of the two fluctuations. Fractions add to one by definition. When the net correlation is small, individual fractions can be far above 1 or below 0, as in the figure, because the quadrants have large opposite contributions that nearly cancel.

worked.title: Check the quadrant bars add up
worked.problem: The bars read about -0.86 (outward interaction), +1.48 (ejection), -1.18 (inward interaction) and +1.56 (sweep). Do they satisfy the sum rule, and what does the size of the individual bars say about the net shear stress?

solution.text: The positive bars together are 3.04 and the negative bars together are minus 2.04.

worked.answer: The bars sum to 1, as they must. The gross contribution is about five times the net, so the net shear stress is a small difference of large terms.

analyze.q: The Q-criterion panel and the Okubo-Weiss panel carry the same information in 2D. Why might the authors still show both?
analyze.hint: Names, thresholds and colour choices are different.

analyze.q: The Q-R histogram is so concentrated that its tails are invisible on a linear colour scale. What display change would show the shape of the distribution?
analyze.hint: Log counts or a contour of the joint PDF.

analyze.q: The quadrant fractions are +1.48 and +1.56 for the two classes that carry the net stress. A reader says 'ejections and sweeps dominate, as in a wall layer'. Respond.
analyze.hint: No mean shear and no wall in the data.

evaluate.q: Which statement is best supported by the segmentation figure: 'the vortices are the energy-containing structures', or 'the vortices are where rotation exceeds strain at one instant'? Why?
evaluate.hint: The figure has no energy, time or tracking information.

evaluate.q: Would you trust a vortex count made from this figure? What do you need to fix?

create: Add to the segmentation panel a contour of W at three stated thresholds and a small table of the area fraction of vortex cells at each, so that the dependence on threshold is visible.
Draw the Q-R plot for a 3D field and for a 2D field side by side, with log colour for counts and the discriminant curve overlaid, to show what changes in 2D.

checks.q: Why is a region with high vorticity not necessarily a vortex?
checks.answer: Vorticity measures local rotation including the rotation that goes with pure shear. In a shear layer vorticity is large but the streamlines are not closed. A vortex needs rotation to dominate strain, which is what Q or the Okubo-Weiss parameter test.

checks.q: At one grid point u_x = 1, u_y = 2, v_x = -3 in an incompressible 2D flow. Compute W and Q and state whether the point is a vortex.
checks.answer: W = 4(1 + 2*(-3)) = 4(-5) = -20, and Q = -W/4 = 5. W is negative and Q positive, so rotation dominates: the point is vortex-like.

checks.q: Why would a 2D field have all its Q-R points on the Q axis?
checks.hint: What is the determinant of the 3 by 3 gradient matrix when one row is zero?
checks.answer: The third invariant is minus the determinant. With no z-velocity and no z-dependence the third row and column of the gradient matrix are zero, so the determinant is zero and R = 0 everywhere.

checks.q: Two groups segment the same field with different thresholds and report different numbers of vortices. Is either wrong?
checks.hint: The result depends on a modelling choice.
checks.answer: Not necessarily. Both are answers to different questions, because the threshold defines what counts as a vortex. They are only comparable when the threshold, the smoothing and the resolution are the same, so the threshold is part of the result and must be reported.

checks.q: How would you make the quadrant plot meaningful for a flow with a small net shear stress?
checks.answer: Normalise each quadrant by a stable quantity, such as the product of the standard deviations of u and v, rather than by the small net stress. Then the four bars are comparable in size and sign, and their sum is the correlation coefficient.
